learn.hook: Of all the planets we know, only one has mangoes, monsoon frogs and you. What makes the Earth so special?
points: The Earth has four spheres: the lithosphere (rocks, soil and land), the hydrosphere (oceans, rivers, lakes, ice and groundwater), the atmosphere (air) and the biosphere (all living things).
The biosphere is the narrow zone where land, water and air meet and life is possible. It stretches from the deep ocean floor to the lower part of the atmosphere.
The Earth is the only planet known to support life. It is at the right distance from the Sun, so it has liquid water and suitable temperatures, and its atmosphere has oxygen and an ozone layer.
The spheres are linked: plants take carbon dioxide and give out oxygen, roots break rocks and help form soil, and the water cycle connects the oceans, the air and the land.

Living things are called biotic components; non-living things like sunlight, air, water and soil are abiotic components. Human actions like cutting forests and polluting rivers affect all four spheres.

example.q: Think it through: Look at a village pond with lotus plants, fish and frogs. Which of the four spheres can you find there?
steps: The water of the pond belongs to the hydrosphere.
The mud and soil at the bottom and banks belong to the lithosphere.
The air above the water and the air dissolved in it belong to the atmosphere.
The lotus plants, fish, frogs and tiny organisms belong to the biosphere. So all four spheres meet in the pond.
example.answer: All four: hydrosphere, lithosphere, atmosphere and biosphere.

learn.reallife: When you plant a sapling on Van Mahotsav, you add to the biosphere and it helps the atmosphere and the soil too.

games.title: Spheres of the Earth: true or false?
items: The biosphere is the zone where land, water and air meet and support life.
Life exists where the three other spheres meet and interact.
Groundwater is part of the hydrosphere.
The hydrosphere includes all water: oceans, rivers, lakes, ice and water under the ground.
The biosphere extends to the top of the exosphere.
Life is found only up to the lower atmosphere, not in the thin outer layers.
Soil is a biotic component of an ecosystem.
Soil is non-living (abiotic), though it contains many living organisms.
Green plants add oxygen to the atmosphere.
During photosynthesis plants give out oxygen.
The Earth is the only planet known to support life.
So far, life has not been found anywhere else in the universe.

quiz.q: What is the biosphere?
options: The layer of gases around the Earth
The zone of the Earth where land, water and air meet and life exists
The solid rocky crust of the Earth
The water in oceans, rivers and lakes
quiz.explain: The biosphere is the life zone, where the lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere interact to support living things.
steps: The biosphere is the sphere of all living things.
It is the narrow zone where land, water and air meet and life exists.
Answer: The zone of the Earth where land, water and air meet and life exists
quiz.mistake: Confuses the biosphere with one of the other spheres

quiz.q: Mountains, rocks and soil are part of the:
quiz.explain: 'Litho' means stone. The lithosphere is the solid outer part of the Earth, including landforms and soil.
steps: 'Litho' means stone.
Rocks, soil and landforms belong to the lithosphere.
Answer: Lithosphere
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the names of the spheres

quiz.q: Oceans, rivers, glaciers and groundwater together form the:
quiz.explain: 'Hydro' means water. All the water on the Earth, liquid or frozen, makes up the hydrosphere.
steps: 'Hydro' means water.
All water, liquid or frozen, forms the hydrosphere.
Answer: Hydrosphere
quiz.mistake: Forgets that ice and groundwater are also part of the hydrosphere

quiz.q: Why is the Earth able to support life?
options: It is the largest planet in the solar system
It is the planet closest to the Sun
It has liquid water, suitable temperatures and air with oxygen
It has no atmosphere to block sunlight
quiz.explain: The Earth's distance from the Sun gives temperatures at which water stays liquid, and its atmosphere has oxygen and protective ozone.
steps: The Earth is at the right distance from the Sun for liquid water and suitable temperatures.
Its air also has oxygen and an ozone layer, so it supports life.
Answer: It has liquid water, suitable temperatures and air with oxygen
quiz.mistake: Thinks size or closeness to the Sun is what makes life possible

quiz.q: Which of these is a biotic component?
quiz.explain: Biotic means living. Earthworms are living things; sunlight, water and sand are abiotic (non-living).
steps: Biotic means living; abiotic means non-living.
Earthworms are alive, while sunlight, rainwater and sand are not.
Answer: Earthworms in the soil
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything found in nature is biotic

quiz.q: How do green plants change the atmosphere?
options: They take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen
They take in oxygen and give out only nitrogen
They remove all water vapour from the air
They have no effect on the air
quiz.explain: In photosynthesis, plants use carbon dioxide and release oxygen, linking the biosphere with the atmosphere.
steps: In photosynthesis plants use carbon dioxide.
They give out oxygen, changing the atmosphere.
Answer: They take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen
quiz.mistake: Reverses the gases taken in and given out in photosynthesis

quiz.q: Which example shows the biosphere changing the lithosphere?
options: Wind blowing clouds across the sky
Roots of a peepal tree cracking a rock
quiz.explain: Roots are living (biosphere) and they break rock (lithosphere). The other examples do not involve living things.
steps: The example must have a living thing acting on rock.
Peepal roots (biosphere) cracking rock (lithosphere) is that case.
Answer: Roots of a peepal tree cracking a rock
quiz.mistake: Does not check whether a living thing is involved

quiz.q: The biosphere reaches from the deep ocean floor up to the:
quiz.explain: Living things are found from the deepest seas to the lower atmosphere, where birds, insects and spores can float. Higher up the air is too thin and cold.
steps: Life is found from the deepest seas to the air where birds and spores float.
Higher up the air is too thin and cold, so the limit is the lower atmosphere.
Answer: lower part of the atmosphere
quiz.mistake: Imagines life extends through all layers of the atmosphere or deep into the Earth

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: "I live in a tree, drink from a river and fly in the air. Which sphere do I belong to?"
teach.praise: Chirp! I belong to the biosphere, but I need the lithosphere, the hydrosphere and the atmosphere to live. All four spheres work together!
teach.nudge: Hmm, what are the other spheres, and where do they meet to make life possible?

revise.summary: The Earth has four spheres — lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere. The biosphere is the narrow life zone where they meet. The Earth supports life because it has liquid water, suitable temperatures and oxygen, and all the spheres are linked.
focus: The four spheres of the Earth
remember: Lithosphere = land, rocks, soil; hydrosphere = all water; atmosphere = air; biosphere = living things
Biosphere stretches from the deep ocean floor to the lower atmosphere
Earth is the only planet known to support life — liquid water, suitable temperatures, oxygen, ozone
Biotic = living; abiotic = sunlight, air, water, soil
traps: Sunlight and water are abiotic, not biotic.
A mushroom is not a producer; it is a decomposer.

learn.hook: In the grasslands of a national park, a deer eats grass and a tiger hunts the deer. When the tiger dies, mushrooms and bacteria recycle it. Everyone is connected!
points: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with each other and with their non-living surroundings (sunlight, air, water, soil). A pond, a forest and a desert are all ecosystems.

Producers (green plants, algae) make food from sunlight. Consumers eat others: herbivores are primary consumers, carnivores that eat them are secondary consumers, and so on. Omnivores eat both plants and animals.
Decomposers like bacteria and fungi break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil.

A food chain shows who eats whom, for example grass → deer → tiger. Many linked food chains form a food web. Energy flows one way from the Sun, and only about 10% passes to the next level, so food chains are short. Nutrients keep cycling.

Ecosystems are terrestrial (forest, grassland, desert) or aquatic (freshwater, marine). Large areas with similar climate, plants and animals are called biomes: forest, grassland, desert, aquatic and altitudinal (high mountain) biomes.

example.q: Think it through: In the food chain grass → deer → tiger, the grass stores 10,000 units of energy. About how much reaches the tiger?
steps: Only about 10% of the energy passes from one level to the next.
Grass to deer: 10% of 10,000 = 1,000 units.
Deer to tiger: 10% of 1,000 = 100 units.

learn.reallife: A school kitchen garden, a village pond and even a fish tank at home are small ecosystems. Compost pits work because of decomposers.

games.title: Build the food chain
games.prompt: Arrange from producer to top consumer

items.q: Green plants are producers or consumers?
A deer that eats only plants is a?
Bacteria and fungi that break down dead matter are called?
The main source of energy for almost all ecosystems?
About what percent of energy passes to the next level?
Many linked food chains form a food ___?
An animal that eats both plants and animals is an?

quiz.q: What is an ecosystem?
options: Living things interacting with each other and with their non-living surroundings
Only the animals living in a forest
Only the soil and water of a place
A list of all plants in India
quiz.explain: An ecosystem includes both biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) parts and the way they interact.
steps: An ecosystem has living and non-living parts.
It is living things interacting with each other and with their non-living surroundings.
Answer: Living things interacting with each other and with their non-living surroundings
quiz.mistake: Thinks an ecosystem includes only living things or only non-living things

quiz.q: Which of these is a producer?
quiz.explain: Green plants like the neem tree make their own food by photosynthesis, so they are producers. A mushroom is a fungus, a decomposer.
steps: Producers make their own food from sunlight.
A neem tree is a green plant, so it is a producer; a mushroom is a decomposer.
Answer: A neem tree
quiz.mistake: Thinks mushrooms are plants that make their own food

quiz.q: What is the role of decomposers such as bacteria and fungi?
options: They break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil
quiz.explain: Decomposers recycle nutrients. Without them, dead material would pile up and soil would lose its nutrients.
steps: Bacteria and fungi break down dead plants and animals.
This returns nutrients to the soil.
Answer: They break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil
quiz.mistake: Confuses decomposers with producers or predators

quiz.q: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, the frog is a:
quiz.explain: The grasshopper eats grass (primary consumer). The frog eats the grasshopper, so it is a secondary consumer.
steps: Grass is the producer and the grasshopper eating it is the primary consumer.
The frog eats the grasshopper, so it is a secondary consumer.
Answer: secondary consumer
quiz.mistake: Counts the levels wrongly or calls every animal a primary consumer

quiz.q: In grass → deer → tiger, the grass has 10,000 units of energy. With about 10% passed on at each step, how many units reach the tiger?
quiz.explain: Grass to deer: 10% of 10,000 = 1,000. Deer to tiger: 10% of 1,000 = 100.
quiz.mistake: Applies the 10% rule only once or not at all
steps: Deer gets 10% of 10,000 = 1,000
Tiger gets 10% of 1,000 = 100
Answer: 100

quiz.q: What is the main source of energy for almost all ecosystems?
quiz.explain: Producers capture sunlight to make food, and that energy then passes along the food chain.
steps: Producers capture sunlight to make food.
That energy passes along the food chain, so the Sun is the main source.
Answer: The Sun
quiz.mistake: Thinks plants get their energy from soil or water

quiz.q: Which of these is an aquatic ecosystem?
quiz.explain: Aquatic ecosystems are water-based, like ponds, lakes, rivers and seas. The others are terrestrial (land-based).
steps: Aquatic ecosystems are water-based.
A pond is aquatic; grassland, desert and forest are terrestrial.
Answer: A pond
quiz.mistake: Mixes up terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems

quiz.q: Why are most food chains short, with only 3 to 5 levels?
options: Animals do not like to eat each other
Decomposers eat the top consumers first
Most energy is lost at each level, so little is left for higher levels
Plants make less food every year
quiz.explain: Only about 10% of energy passes to the next level, so after a few steps there is too little to support another level.
steps: Only about 10% of energy passes to the next level.
After a few steps too little is left, so food chains are short.
Answer: Most energy is lost at each level, so little is left for higher levels
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the length of food chains with energy loss

teach.ask: Gappu pecks a seed and asks: "Who eats whom in a forest, and what happens to animals and plants after they die?"
teach.praise: Tweet! Plants make food from sunlight, animals eat plants or each other, and decomposers recycle everything. What a team!
teach.nudge: Nice! But who starts the food chain, and who cleans up when things die?

revise.summary: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with each other and their surroundings. Producers, consumers and decomposers are linked through food chains and food webs. Energy flows one way from the Sun and only about 10% passes on at each level.
focus: Biotic and abiotic parts of an ecosystem
Food chains, food webs and energy flow
remember: Producers: green plants, algae; decomposers: bacteria, fungi
Herbivores = primary consumers; carnivores eating them = secondary consumers
Food chain example: grass → deer → tiger
About 10% of energy passes to the next level; nutrients keep cycling
traps: Energy flows one way; it does not cycle like nutrients.
In grass → grasshopper → frog, the frog is a secondary consumer, not primary.

learn.hook: India has more than a thousand varieties of mango, hundreds of kinds of rice and animals found nowhere else on Earth. That variety is called biodiversity.
points: Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth. It exists at three levels: genetic diversity (variety within a species, like many types of rice or mango), species diversity and ecosystem diversity.
India is one of the world's 17 megadiverse countries. With only about 2.4% of the world's land area, it has about 7 to 8% of the recorded species.

India has parts of four of the world's 36 biodiversity hotspots: the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (the Nicobar Islands). Endemic species found only in a region include the lion-tailed macaque and the Nilgiri tahr of the Western Ghats.
Threats: loss of habitat as forests are cleared, poaching, pollution, invasive species like lantana and water hyacinth, and climate change.

Conservation: in-situ (in natural homes: national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves) and ex-situ (outside: zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks). India passed the Wildlife (Protection) Act in 1972 and started Project Tiger in 1973. Communities help too: the Bishnois of Rajasthan protect blackbuck and khejri trees, and in the Chipko movement villagers hugged trees to save them.

example.q: Think it through: Why does saving the tiger help save the whole forest?
steps: A tiger needs a large, healthy forest with plenty of deer and other prey.
To protect tigers, the forest, its grasslands and its water sources must all be protected.
The tiger, as a top predator, also keeps the number of deer in balance, so plants are not overgrazed.
So protecting one tiger protects thousands of other plants and animals in its home.
example.answer: Protecting tigers means protecting their whole habitat, and tigers keep the food web in balance.

learn.reallife: When you visit Gir to see the Asiatic lion or Kaziranga to see the one-horned rhinoceros, you are visiting places set up for in-situ conservation.

items.text: The variety of all life on Earth is called ___.
National parks protect species in their ___ habitat.
Zoos and seed banks are examples of ___ conservation.
The ___ community of Rajasthan is known for protecting blackbuck and khejri trees.

quiz.q: What does biodiversity mean?
options: The number of rivers in a country
The study of rocks and soil
The variety of all living things in an area or on Earth
quiz.explain: Biodiversity covers the variety of genes, species and ecosystems.
steps: Bio means life and diversity means variety.
Biodiversity is the variety of all living things, at gene, species and ecosystem levels.
Answer: The variety of all living things in an area or on Earth
quiz.mistake: Thinks biodiversity is about non-living features or only humans

quiz.q: Farmers in India grow hundreds of varieties of rice. Which level of biodiversity does this show?
quiz.explain: All rice varieties belong to the same species; the differences between them are genetic diversity.
steps: All rice varieties belong to one species.
Variety within a species is genetic diversity.
Answer: Genetic diversity
quiz.mistake: Thinks different varieties are different species

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of in-situ conservation?
quiz.explain: In-situ means 'in the original place'. National parks protect plants and animals in their natural habitat. The others are ex-situ.
steps: In-situ means in the original place.
A national park protects life in its natural home; zoos, seed banks and gardens are ex-situ.
Answer: A national park
quiz.mistake: Mixes up in-situ and ex-situ conservation

quiz.q: Where are Asiatic lions found in the wild today?
quiz.explain: The Gir forest and nearby areas of Gujarat are the only place in the world where Asiatic lions live in the wild.
steps: Asiatic lions survive in the wild in only one place.
That is the Gir forest in Gujarat.
Answer: Gir forest in Gujarat
quiz.mistake: Confuses the home of the lion with that of the tiger or rhinoceros

quiz.q: Which of these is a biodiversity hotspot that lies partly in India?
quiz.explain: The Western Ghats and Sri Lanka hotspot is rich in species found nowhere else. India also has parts of the Himalaya, Indo-Burma and Sundaland hotspots.
steps: India has parts of four hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland.
So the Western Ghats is the hotspot among the options.
Answer: Western Ghats
quiz.mistake: Thinks any large region of India is a hotspot

quiz.q: In which year was Project Tiger launched in India?
quiz.explain: Project Tiger began in 1973 to protect tigers and their habitats. Project Elephant began later, in 1992.
steps: India passed the Wildlife (Protection) Act in 1972.
Project Tiger started the next year, in 1973.
Answer: 1973
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Project Tiger with Project Elephant or Independence

quiz.q: Which of these is a major threat to biodiversity?
options: Clearing forests for new farms and roads
quiz.explain: Habitat loss is one of the biggest threats, because plants and animals lose their homes and food.
steps: Habitat loss is one of the biggest threats.
Clearing forests for farms and roads destroys homes and food of plants and animals.
Answer: Clearing forests for new farms and roads
quiz.mistake: Picks a conservation action instead of a threat

quiz.q: The Chipko movement is remembered because villagers:
options: started a seed bank in a city
hugged trees to stop them from being cut down
quiz.explain: In the Chipko movement of the 1970s in the Himalayan region of present-day Uttarakhand, villagers, many of them women, hugged trees to prevent felling.
steps: Chipko means to hug or cling.
Villagers hugged trees to stop them from being cut down.
Answer: hugged trees to stop them from being cut down
quiz.mistake: Does not know what the Chipko movement did

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "Why should we care if one small frog or flower disappears? There are so many others!"
teach.praise: Squawk! Every species is linked in the food web, so losing one hurts others. Protecting habitats in national parks keeps the variety alive!
teach.nudge: But how is that frog connected to other living things, and what can we do to protect it?

revise.summary: Biodiversity is the variety of life at genetic, species and ecosystem levels. India is megadiverse and has parts of four hotspots. Habitat loss, poaching, pollution and invasive species threaten it; in-situ and ex-situ conservation, laws and communities help protect it.
focus: India as a megadiverse country and its hotspots
In-situ and ex-situ conservation and community efforts
remember: India: about 2.4% of world land, about 7–8% of recorded species; one of 17 megadiverse countries
Hotspots in India: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Sundaland (Nicobar)
In-situ: national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves; ex-situ: zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks
Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972; Project Tiger 1973; Bishnois and Chipko movement
traps: Zoos and seed banks are ex-situ, not in-situ.
Many rice varieties show genetic diversity, not species diversity.
